Language Comparison

Java, C, C++, Python and JavaScript compared property by property, with a conclusion on which language fits which job.

The concept

Programming languages differ in how they run (compiled to machine code or bytecode, or interpreted), how they manage memory (manual or garbage collected) and what they are best at.

Java is compiled to bytecode that runs on the JVM, so the same program runs on Windows, Linux or macOS: write once, run anywhere. C and C++ give direct hardware control, Python is quick to write and dominates AI, and JavaScript runs in every browser.

Java Installation

Installing the JDK on Windows (OpenJDK and Oracle JDK), setting JAVA_HOME and PATH, and running the first Hello program.

The concept

The JDK (Java Development Kit) contains the compiler javac, the runtime JRE/JVM that executes programs, and other tools. Source files (.java) are compiled into bytecode (.class) and then run with java.

JAVA_HOME stores the JDK folder, and adding %JAVA_HOME%\bin to PATH lets Command Prompt find java and javac from any folder.

Installing OpenJDK on Windows

Software required: Windows OS, internet connection, OpenJDK, Command Prompt.

Step 1: Download OpenJDK
  1. Open any web browser.
  2. Visit the official OpenJDK or Eclipse Adoptium website.
  3. Download the latest stable OpenJDK for Windows (64-bit).
Step 2: Install OpenJDK
  1. Double-click the downloaded installer.
  2. Follow the installation wizard and choose the install location if required.
  3. Click Install, wait, then click Finish.
Step 3: Set JAVA_HOME and PATH
  1. Press Windows + R, type sysdm.cpl, press Enter.
  2. Advanced tab → Environment Variables → under System Variables click New.
  3. Name JAVA_HOME, value e.g. C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-21.
  4. Select Path → Edit → New → add %JAVA_HOME%\bin → OK.
Step 4: Verify the installation
  1. Open Command Prompt and run java --version → openjdk 21.0.11.
  2. Run javac --version → javac 21.0.11.
Hello World program

Hello.java (OpenJDK)

Source code · Hello.java
public class Hello {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello World");
    }
}
Output
Hello World

Compile with javac Hello.java (creates Hello.class), run with java Hello.

Installing Oracle JDK on Windows

Software required: Windows OS, internet connection, Java Development Kit (JDK).

Step 1: Download
  1. Open a web browser and visit the official Oracle JDK downloads page.
  2. Download the latest JDK for Windows (e.g. JDK 25).
Step 2: Install
  1. Double-click the downloaded .exe file.
  2. Click Next, follow the wizard and finish.
Step 3: Verify
  1. Command Prompt → java --version → java 25.0.3.
  2. javac --version → javac 25.0.3.
Configuring JAVA_HOME and PATH

Find the JDK folder, e.g. C:\Program Files\Java\jdk-25.0.3, then create the system variable:

Next edit Path → New → %JAVA_HOME%\bin → OK → OK → OK.

The concept

A Java program is a class with a main method. Data is stored in variables of a given type, combined with operators, converted between types, and controlled with decision and loop statements.

Getting Started

Every program is compiled with javac and run with java. Output is printed with System.out.println().

Data Types and Variables

Java has 8 primitive types:

  • byte (8-bit), short (16), int (32), long (64) for whole numbers
  • float (32) and double (64) for decimals
  • char (16-bit Unicode) and boolean (true/false)

A variable is a named memory location that must be declared with a type before use.

Primitive Data Types

Java has 8 primitives: byte, short, int, long (integers), float, double (decimals), char (16-bit Unicode) and boolean.

Operators and Expressions

Arithmetic operators + - * / % work on integers and decimals. Integer division drops the fraction, while % returns the remainder. Swapping two variables needs a temporary variable.

Arithmetic Operations on Integers

Operators + - * / %. Integer division discards the fraction; % gives the remainder.

Aim

Procedure
  1. Aim: To perform arithmetic operations on two integer variables.
  2. Declare two integer variables.
  3. Perform addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulus operations.
  4. Display the results.

  6. Result: The arithmetic operations on integer variables were performed successfully.
Source code
public class calculator {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 50, b = 10;
        System.out.println("Addition      : " + (a + b));
        System.out.println("Subtraction   : " + (a - b));
        System.out.println("Multiplication: " + (a * b));
        System.out.println("Division      : " + (a / b));
        System.out.println("Modulus       : " + (a % b));
    }
}

Addition      : 60
Subtraction   : 40
Multiplication: 500
Division      : 5

Arithmetic Operations on Floating-Point Numbers

float/double keep fractions; double has about 15 digits of precision, float about 7.

Aim

Procedure
  1. Aim: To perform arithmetic operations using floating-point numbers.
  2. Declare two floating-point variables.
  3. Perform basic arithmetic operations.
  4. Display the results.
  5. Compile and execute the program.
  6. Result: The arithmetic operations on floating-point numbers were executed successfully.
Source code
public class floatingpoint {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double x = 1.50, y = 2.00;
        System.out.printf("Addition (1.50 + 2.00)       = %.2f%n", x + y);
        System.out.printf("Subtraction (1.50 - 2.00)    = %.2f%n", x - y);
        System.out.printf("Multiplication (1.50 * 2.00) = %.2f%n", x * y);
        System.out.printf("Division (1.50 / 2.00)       = %.4f%n", x / y);
        System.out.printf("Modulo (1.50 %% 2.00)         = %.2f%n", x % y);
    }
}
Output
Addition (1.50 + 2.00)       = 3.50
Subtraction (1.50 - 2.00)    = -0.50
Multiplication (1.50 * 2.00) = 3.00
Division (1.50 / 2.00)       = 0.7500
Modulo (1.50 % 2.00)         = 1.50
Result

Swapping Two Variables

A temporary variable holds one value so neither is overwritten while swapping.

Aim

Procedure
  1. Aim: To swap the values of two variables using a temporary variable.
  2. Declare two variables.
  3. Use a temporary variable to swap their values.
  4. Display the values before and after swapping.
  5. Compile and run the program.
  6. Result: The values of the two variables were swapped successfully.
Source code
public class swapping {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 5, b = 10, temp;
        System.out.println("Before Swapping:");
        System.out.println("Value 1 = " + a);
        System.out.println("Value 2 = " + b);
        temp = a;
        a = b;
        b = temp;
        System.out.println("after Swapping:");
        System.out.println("Value 1 = " + a);
        System.out.println("Value 2 = " + b);
    }
}
Output
Before Swapping:
Value 1 = 5
Value 2 = 10
after Swapping:
Value 1 = 10
Value 2 = 5
Result

Type Conversion and Casting

Widening (automatic): a smaller type goes into a larger one without loss, byte → short → int → long → float → double.

Narrowing (explicit cast): a larger type is forced into a smaller one with (type); the fraction is truncated or the value can wrap around.

Widening Type Conversion

Automatic, lossless conversion to a larger type: byte → short → int → long → float → double.

Aim

Procedure
  1. Aim: To demonstrate automatic (widening) type conversion.
  2. Declare variables of smaller data types.
  3. Assign them to larger data types.
  4. Display the converted values.
  5. Compile and execute the program.
  6. Result: Automatic type conversion was performed successfully.
Source code
public class widconver {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        byte b = 42;
        short s = b;      // byte -> short
        int i = s;        // short -> int
        long l = i;       // int -> long
        float f = l;      // long -> float
        double d = f;     // float -> double
        System.out.println("Original byte value: " + b);
        System.out.println("Widened to short:    " + s);
        System.out.println("Widened to int:      " + i);
        System.out.println("Widened to long:     " + l);
        System.out.println("Widened to float:    " + f);
        System.out.println("Widened to double:   " + d);
        char c = 'A';
        int code = c;     // char -> int
        System.out.println("Original char value: " + c);
        System.out.println("Widened to int:      " + code);
    }
}
Output
Original byte value: 42
Widened to short:    42
Widened to int:      42
Widened to long:     42
Widened to float:    42.0
Widened to double:   42.0
Original char value: A
Widened to int:      65
Result

Narrowing Type Casting

Explicit cast to a smaller type, e.g. (int) 9.7 gives 9. Data can be truncated.

Aim

Procedure
  1. Aim: To demonstrate explicit (narrowing) type casting.
  2. Declare a variable of a larger data type.
  3. Convert it to a smaller data type using type casting.
  4. Display the converted value.
  5. Compile and run the program.
  6. Result: Explicit type casting was demonstrated successfully.
Source code
public class narconver {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double d = 99.99;
        int i = (int) d;          // fraction is truncated
        System.out.println("Original double value: " + d);
        System.out.println("Narrowed int value   : " + i);
        int big = 130;
        byte b = (byte) big;      // 130 does not fit in a byte, wraps to -126
        System.out.println("Original int value   : " + big);
        System.out.println("Narrowed byte value  : " + b);
        int code = 65;
        char c = (char) code;
        System.out.println("Original int value   : " + code);
        System.out.println("Narrowed char value  : " + c);
    }
}
Output
Original double value: 99.99
Narrowed int value   : 99
Original int value   : 130
Narrowed byte value  : -126
Original int value   : 65
Narrowed char value  : A
Result

Control Statements

if-else chooses between paths using a boolean condition; the for loop repeats a block a known number of times.

Even or Odd

n % 2 == 0 inside an if-else decides parity.

Aim

Procedure
  1. Aim: To check whether a given number is even or odd using the if-else statement.
  2. Declare an integer variable.
  3. Use an if-else statement to check whether the number is even or odd.
  4. Display the result.
  5. Compile and run the program.
  6. Result: The program correctly identified whether the number was even or odd.
Source code
public class evenodd {
    static void check(int n) {
        if (n % 2 == 0)
        System.out.println(n + " is an even number.");
        else
        System.out.println(n + " is an odd number.");
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        check(5);
        check(10);
    }
}
Output
5 is an odd number.
10 is an even number.
Result

Java Reserved Keywords

Words such as class, int, static are reserved and cannot be identifiers; the compiler rejects them.

Aim

Procedure
  1. Aim: To demonstrate the use of Java reserved keywords and understand why they cannot be used as variable names.
  2. Create valid variable names.
  3. Observe that Java keywords cannot be used as identifiers.
  4. Compile and execute the program.
  5. Note the output or compiler behavior.
  6. Result: The program demonstrated the use of valid identifiers and the restriction on Java keywords.
Source code
public class keyword {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int number = 10;        // valid identifier
        String name = "Java";   // valid identifier
        // Reserved words cannot be used as variable names:
        int class = 10;
        double if = 5.5;
        String while = "Java";
    }
}

Keywords and Identifiers

Keywords such as class, if and while are reserved by the language and cannot be used as variable names; the compiler reports an error.

Classes, Objects and OOP

Experiments 1–14: class fundamentals, objects, references, methods, constructors, this, garbage collection, overloading, static, final, nested and inner classes.

The concept

Object-oriented programming models real things as classes (blueprints) and objects (instances). A class bundles data (fields) with behaviour (methods); objects are created with new and initialised by constructors.

Class Fundamentals

A class declares fields and methods; new creates an object of it.

Student Information System

Source code
class Student {
    int rollNo;
    String name;
    String branch;
    double cgpa;
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Roll Number: " + rollNo);
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("Branch: " + branch);
        System.out.println("CGPA: " + cgpa);
    }
}
public class StudentInfo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s = new Student();
        s.rollNo = 101;
        s.name = "Raina";
        s.branch = "CSE-AIML";
        s.cgpa = 9.2;
        s.display();
    }
}
Output
Roll Number: 101
Name: Raina
Branch: CSE-AIML
CGPA: 9.2

Declaring Objects

Declaring a reference and creating the object are two steps; several objects, or an array of objects, can share one class.

Assigning Object Reference Variables

Assigning one object reference to another copies the reference, not the object, so both names point to the same object.

Reference Assignment

Source code
class Student {
    String name;
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
    }
}
public class ReferenceAssignment {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s1 = new Student();
        s1.name = "Raina";
        Student s2 = s1;
        System.out.println("Before modification:");
        s2.display();
        s1.name = "Rinku";
        System.out.println("After modification:");
        s2.display();
    }
}
Output
Before modification:
Name: Raina
After modification:
Name: Rinku

Comparing Object References

Source code
class Employee {
    int id;
    String name;
    Employee(int id, String name) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
    }
}
public class CompareReferences {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Employee e1 = new Employee(101, "Rahul");
        Employee e2 = e1;
        if (e1 == e2) {
            System.out.println("Both references point to the same object.");
        } else {
            System.out.println("References point to different objects.");
        }
    }
}
Output
Both references point to the same object.

Introducing Methods

A method groups reusable behaviour; it can take parameters and return a value.

Calculator Using Methods

Source code
class Calculator {
    int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
    int subtract(int a, int b) {
        return a - b;
    }
    int multiply(int a, int b) {
        return a * b;
    }
    double divide(int a, int b) {
        return (double) a / b;
    }
}
public class CalculatorDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Calculator c = new Calculator();
        int a = 20;
        int b = 10;
        System.out.println("Addition: " + c.add(a, b));
        System.out.println("Subtraction: " + c.subtract(a, b));
        System.out.println("Multiplication: " + c.multiply(a, b));
        System.out.println("Division: " + c.divide(a, b));
    }
}
Output
Addition: 30
Subtraction: 10
Multiplication: 200
Division: 2.0

class Rectangle {

Constructors

A constructor has the class name, no return type, and runs when the object is created. Several constructors with different parameters are called constructor overloading.

Student Constructors

Source code
class Student {
    String name;
    int rollNo;
    Student() {
        name = "Unknown";
        rollNo = 0;
    }
    Student(String name, int rollNo) {
        this.name = name;
        this.rollNo = rollNo;
    }
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("Roll Number: " + rollNo);
    }
}
public class StudentConstructor {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s1 = new Student();
        Student s2 = new Student("Raina", 101);
        System.out.println("Default Constructor:");
        s1.display();
        System.out.println("\nParameterized Constructor:");
        s2.display();
    }
}
Output
Default Constructor:
Name: Unknown
Roll Number: 0
Parameterized Constructor:
Name: Raina
Roll Number: 101

Constructor Overloading

Source code
class BankAccount {

        accountNo = 0;

        b1.display();
        b2.display();
        b3.display();

}
Output

Name: Unknown
Balance: 0.0
Account Number: 101
Name: Raina
Balance: 0.0
Account Number: 102

this refers to the current object. It separates fields from parameters of the same name, and this(...) chains one constructor to another.

    }
}
public class ThisDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

Source code
class Student {

Garbage Collection

Java frees memory automatically: objects with no references become eligible for the garbage collector. System.gc() only requests a run.

Demonstrating Garbage Collection

Source code
class Demo {
    int id;
    Demo(int id) {
        this.id = id;
    }
    protected void finalize() {
        System.out.println("Object " + id + " is garbage collected.");
    }
}
public class GarbageCollectionDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Demo d1 = new Demo(1);
        Demo d2 = new Demo(2);
        Demo d3 = new Demo(3);
        d1 = null;
        d2 = null;
        d3 = null;
        System.gc();
        System.out.println("Garbage collection requested.");
    }
}
Output
Garbage collection requested.

Object Eligibility for Garbage Collection

Source code
class Demo {
    int id;
    Demo(int id) {
        this.id = id;
    }
}
public class ObjectEligibility {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Demo d1 = new Demo(1);
        d1 = null;
        Demo d2 = new Demo(2);
        d2 = new Demo(3);
        new Demo(4);
        System.gc();
        System.out.println("Objects are eligible for garbage collection.");
    }
}
Output
Objects are eligible for garbage collection.

Method Overloading

Overloading means several methods with the same name but different parameter lists (compile-time polymorphism).

Overloading Arithmetic Methods

Source code
class Calculator {
    int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
    int add(int a, int b, int c) {
        return a + b + c;
    }
    double add(double a, double b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}
public class ArithmeticOverloading {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Calculator c = new Calculator();
        System.out.println("Two integers: " + c.add(10, 20));
        System.out.println("Three integers: " + c.add(10, 20, 30));
        System.out.println("Two doubles: " + c.add(10.5, 20.5));
    }
}
Output
Two integers: 30
Three integers: 60
Two doubles: 31.0

Overloading Area Methods

Source code
class Area {
    double area(double radius) {
        return Math.PI * radius * radius;
    }
    int area(int length, int width) {
        return length * width;
    }
    int area(int side) {
        return side * side;
    }
}
public class AreaOverloading {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Area a = new Area();
        System.out.println("Circle Area: " + a.area(5.0));
        System.out.println("Rectangle Area: " + a.area(10, 5));
        System.out.println("Square Area: " + a.area(4));
    }
}
Output
Circle Area: 78.53981633974483
Rectangle Area: 50
Square Area: 16

Comparing Employee Salaries

Source code
class Employee {
    String name;
    double salary;
    Employee(String name, double salary) {
        this.name = name;
        this.salary = salary;
    }
}
public class EmployeeSalary {
    static void compare(Employee e1, Employee e2) {
        if (e1.salary > e2.salary) {
            System.out.println(e1.name + " has the higher salary.");
        } else if (e2.salary > e1.salary) {
            System.out.println(e2.name + " has the higher salary.");
        } else {
            System.out.println("Both employees have the same salary.");
        }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Employee e1 = new Employee("Rahul", 50000);
        Employee e2 = new Employee("Ananya", 60000);
        compare(e1, e2);
    }
}
Output
Ananya has the higher salary.

Understanding static

static members belong to the class, not to any object: one shared variable (a counter) and methods called without creating an object.

Static Variable

Source code
class Student {
    String name;
    static int count = 0;
    Student(String name) {
        this.name = name;
        count++;
    }
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
    }
}
public class StaticVariable {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s1 = new Student("Raina");
        Student s2 = new Student("Rinku");
        Student s3 = new Student("Amar");
        s1.display();
        s2.display();
        s3.display();
        System.out.println("Total Students: " + Student.count);
    }
}
Output
Name: Raina
Name: Rinku
Name: Amar
Total Students: 3

Static Methods

Source code
class Utility {
    static int square(int n) {
        return n * n;
    }
    static int cube(int n) {
        return n * n * n;
    }
    static long factorial(int n) {
        long fact = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            fact *= i;
        }
        return fact;
    }
}
public class StaticMethods {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int n = 5;
        System.out.println("Square: " + Utility.square(n));
        System.out.println("Cube: " + Utility.cube(n));
        System.out.println("Factorial: " + Utility.factorial(n));
    }
}
Output
Square: 25
Cube: 125
Factorial: 120

Introducing final

final on a variable makes it a constant, on a method stops overriding, and on a class stops inheritance.

Final Keyword

Source code
class Parent {
    final int VALUE = 100;
    final void display() {
        System.out.println("This is a final method.");
        System.out.println("Final variable: " + VALUE);
    }
}
final class FinalClass {
    void show() {
        System.out.println("This is a final class.");
    }
}
public class FinalDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Parent p = new Parent();
        p.display();
        FinalClass f = new FinalClass();
        f.show();
    }
}
Output
This is a final method.
Final variable: 100
This is a final class.

Strings and Introductory Inheritance

String constructors and the string pool, mutable StringBuffer operations, StringTokenizer, basic inheritance and the super keyword.

The concept

A String is an immutable sequence of characters stored in the String Constant Pool when written as a literal. When text must change often, mutable classes such as StringBuffer are used, and StringTokenizer splits text into tokens.

String Constructors and the String Pool

Strings can be built from literals, char[] or byte[]. Literals with the same text share one object in the String Constant Pool, whereas new String() always creates a separate heap object. == compares references; .equals() compares content.

String Constructors

Source code
public class StringCons{
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String strLiteral1 = "Java";
        String strLiteral2 = "Java";
        String strEmpty = new String();
        char[] charArray = {'P', 'r', 'o', 'g', 'r', 'a', 'm'};
        String strFromChar = new String(charArray);
        byte[] byteArray = {67, 111, 100, 101};
        String strFromByte = new String(byteArray);
        String strNewObject1 = new String("Java");
        String strNewObject2 = new String("Java");
        System.out.println("====================================");
        System.out.println("       DISPLAYING CREATED STRINGS        ");
        System.out.println("====================================");
        System.out.println("1. String Literal: " + strLiteral1);
        System.out.println("2. Empty String via new String(): '" + strEmpty + "' (Length: " + strEmpty.length() + ")");
        System.out.println("3. From Character Array: " + strFromChar);
        System.out.println("4. From Byte Array: " + strFromByte);
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println("=======================================");
        System.out.println("     LITERAL VS NEW KEYWORD DEMO         ");
        System.out.println("=======================================");
        System.out.print("Comparing two literals (strLiteral1 == strLiteral2): ");
        System.out.println(strLiteral1 == strLiteral2);
        System.out.print("Comparing literal with 'new' object (strLiteral1 == strNewObject1): ");
        System.out.println(strLiteral1 == strNewObject1);
        System.out.print("Comparing two 'new' objects (strNewObject1 == strNewObject2): ");
        System.out.println(strNewObject1 == strNewObject2);
        System.out.print("Comparing values using .equals() (strLiteral1.equals(strNewObject1)): ");
        System.out.println(strLiteral1.equals(strNewObject1));
    }
}
Output
======================================
       DISPLAYING CREATED STRINGS
======================================
1. String Literal: Java
2. Empty String via new String(): '' (Length: 0)
3. From Character Array: Program
4. From Byte Array: Code

======================================
     LITERAL VS NEW KEYWORD DEMO
======================================
Comparing two literals (strLiteral1 == strLiteral2): true
Comparing literal with 'new' object (strLiteral1 == strNewObject1): false
Comparing two 'new' objects (strNewObject1 == strNewObject2): false
Comparing values using .equals() (strLiteral1.equals(strNewObject1)): true

StringBuffer

StringBuffer is a mutable, thread-safe string. append, insert, replace, delete and reverse change it in place; it also tracks length and capacity.

StringBuffer Class

Source code
public class StrBuffer{
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StringBuffer sb = new StringBuffer("Hello");
        System.out.println("Initial String: " + sb);
        displayStats(sb);
        sb.append(" World");
        System.out.println("\nAfter Append: " + sb);
        displayStats(sb);
        sb.insert(6, "Beautiful ");
        System.out.println("\nAfter Insert: " + sb);
        displayStats(sb);
        sb.replace(6, 15, "Awesome");
        System.out.println("\nAfter Replace: " + sb);
        displayStats(sb);
        sb.delete(5, 13);
        System.out.println("\nAfter Delete: " + sb);
        displayStats(sb);
        sb.reverse();
        System.out.println("\nAfter Reverse: " + sb);
        displayStats(sb);
    }
    public static void displayStats(StringBuffer buffer) {
        System.out.println("-> Length: " + buffer.length() + " | Capacity: " + buffer.capacity());
    }
}
Output
Initial String: Hello
-> Length: 5 | Capacity: 21
After Append: Hello World
-> Length: 11 | Capacity: 21
After Insert: Hello Beautiful World
-> Length: 21 | Capacity: 21
After Replace: Hello Awesome World
-> Length: 19 | Capacity: 21
After Delete: Hello World
-> Length: 11 | Capacity: 21
After Reverse: dlroW olleH
-> Length: 11 | Capacity: 21

StringTokenizer

StringTokenizer breaks a string into tokens at whitespace or at chosen delimiter characters, and countTokens() tells how many there are.

StringTokenizer Class

Source code
import java.util.Scanner;
import java.util.StringTokenizer;
public class StringTokenizerDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
        System.out.print("Enter a sentence: ");
        String sentence = sc.nextLine();
        StringTokenizer st = new StringTokenizer(sentence);
        int count1 = st.countTokens();
        System.out.println("\nTokens:");
        while (st.hasMoreTokens()) {
            System.out.println(st.nextToken());
        }
        System.out.println("Total number of tokens: " + count1);
        System.out.print("\nEnter a delimiter: ");
        String delimiter = sc.nextLine();
        StringTokenizer st2 = new StringTokenizer(sentence, delimiter);
        int count2 = st2.countTokens();
        System.out.println("\nTokens using delimiter '" + delimiter + "':");
        while (st2.hasMoreTokens()) {
            System.out.println(st2.nextToken());
        }
        System.out.println("Total number of tokens: " + count2);
        sc.close();
    }
}
Output

Tokens:
Java
is
easy
to
learn
Total number of tokens: 5
Enter a delimiter: a
Tokens using delimiter 'a':
J
v
 is e
sy to le
rn
Total number of tokens: 5

Basic Inheritance and super

A subclass inherits fields and methods from its parent. super(...) calls the parent constructor and super.member reaches the parent version.

Basic Inheritance

Source code
class Person {
    String name;
    int age;
    Person(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
    }
    void displayPersonDetails() {

        System.out.println("Age: " + age);
    }
}
class Student extends Person {
    int rollNo;
    String branch;
    Student(String name, int age, int rollNo, String branch) {
        super(name, age);
        this.rollNo = rollNo;
        this.branch = branch;
    }
    void displayStudentDetails() {
        displayPersonDetails();
        System.out.println("Roll Number: " + rollNo);
        System.out.println("Branch: " + branch);
    }
}
public class BasicInheritance {

        s.displayStudentDetails();
    }
}

Age: 19
Roll Number: 101
Branch: CSE-AIML

Inheritance Programs

Single and multilevel inheritance, the super keyword, method overriding, dynamic method dispatch and constructor order.

The concept

Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and extend a superclass with extends, modelling an is-a relationship. It enables method overriding and runtime polymorphism, where the object type, not the reference type, decides which method runs.

Single Inheritance

One subclass extends one superclass and inherits its members; super accesses the parent.

Single Inheritance

Source code
class Person{
    String name="Bhavya";
    int age=19;
}
class Student extends Person{
    int rollno=101;
    String branch="AIML";
    void display(){
        System.out.println("Name: "+super.name);
        System.out.println("Age: "+super.age);
        System.out.println("Roll No: "+rollno);
        System.out.println("Branch: "+branch);
    }
}
public class SInherit{
    public static void main(String[] args){
        Student s1=new Student();
        s1.display();
    }
}
Output
Name: Bhavya
Age: 19
Roll No: 101
Branch: AIML

Using super Keyword

Source code
class Vehicle{
    int speed = 150;
    void display(){
        System.out.println("Speed(Vehicle): "+speed);
    }
}
class Car extends Vehicle{
    String model = "Porsche";
    @Override
    void display(){
        super.display();
        System.out.println("Speed("+model+"): "+super.speed);
    }
}
public class Super{
    public static void main(String[] args){
        Car c = new Car();
        c.display();
    }
}
Output
Speed(Vehicle): 150
Speed(Porsche): 150

Multilevel Inheritance

A chain of classes (grandparent → parent → child). Constructors run from the top of the chain down to the child.

Multilevel Inheritance

Source code
class Person{

Method Overriding

A subclass supplies its own version of an inherited method with the same signature, marked @Override; super.method() can still call the parent version.

Dynamic Method Dispatch

A parent-type reference can hold a child object, and Java picks the overridden method at run time from the actual object, which is runtime polymorphism.

Dynamic Method Dispatch

Source code
class Shape {
    void draw() {
        System.out.println("Drawing a shape");
    }
}
class Circle extends Shape {
    @Override
    void draw() {
        System.out.println("Drawing a Circle");
    }
}
class Rectangle extends Shape {
    @Override
    void draw() {
        System.out.println("Drawing a Rectangle");
    }
}
class Triangle extends Shape {
    @Override
    void draw() {
        System.out.println("Drawing a Triangle");
    }
}
public class Dynamic {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Shape shape;
        shape = new Circle();
        shape.draw();
        shape = new Rectangle();
        shape.draw();
        shape = new Triangle();
        shape.draw();
    }
}
Output
Drawing a Circle
Drawing a Rectangle
Drawing a Triangle

Dynamic Method Dispatch for Bank Accounts

Source code
class BankAccount {
    void calculateInterest() {
        System.out.println("Calculating bank account interest");
    }
}
class SavingsAccount extends BankAccount {
    @Override
    void calculateInterest() {
        System.out.println("Savings Account Interest: 5%");
    }
}
class CurrentAccount extends BankAccount {
    @Override
    void calculateInterest() {
        System.out.println("Current Account Interest: 3%");
    }
}
public class DynamicBankAcc {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BankAccount account;
        account = new SavingsAccount();
        account.calculateInterest();
        account = new CurrentAccount();
        account.calculateInterest();
    }
}
Output
Savings Account Interest: 5%
Current Account Interest: 3%

Application: Banking with Inheritance

Putting it together: a base BankAccount with SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount overriding interest calculation.

Banking Application Using Inheritance

Source code
class BankAccount {
    int accountNumber;
    double balance;
    BankAccount(int accountNumber, double balance) {
        this.accountNumber = accountNumber;
        this.balance = balance;
    }
    void deposit(double amount) {
        balance += amount;
        System.out.println("Deposited: " + amount);
    }
    void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount <= balance) {
            balance -= amount;
            System.out.println("Withdrawn: " + amount);
        } else {
            System.out.println("Insufficient balance");
        }
    }
    void calculateInterest() {
        System.out.println("Interest calculation for Bank Account");
    }
    void displayBalance() {
        System.out.println("Account Number: " + accountNumber);
        System.out.println("Balance: " + balance);
    }
}
class SavingsAccount extends BankAccount {
    SavingsAccount(int accountNumber, double balance) {
        super(accountNumber, balance);
    }
    @Override
    void calculateInterest() {
        double interest = balance * 0.05;
        System.out.println("Savings Account Interest: " + interest);
    }
}
class CurrentAccount extends BankAccount {
    CurrentAccount(int accountNumber, double balance) {
        super(accountNumber, balance);
    }
    @Override
    void calculateInterest() {
        double interest = balance * 0.03;
        System.out.println("Current Account Interest: " + interest);
    }
}
public class BankAppInherit {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SavingsAccount savings = new SavingsAccount(101, 10000);
        System.out.println("Savings Account:");
        savings.deposit(2000);
        savings.withdraw(1000);
        savings.calculateInterest();
        savings.displayBalance();
        System.out.println();
        CurrentAccount current = new CurrentAccount(102, 20000);
        System.out.println("Current Account:");
        current.deposit(5000);
        current.withdraw(3000);
        current.calculateInterest();
        current.displayBalance();
    }
}

Exception Handling

try–catch, multiple catch, throw, throws, finally and user-defined exceptions.

The concept

An exception is an event that disrupts normal flow. Java handles them with try, catch, finally, throw and throws, so a program can recover instead of crashing.

try and catch

Risky code goes in try; the matching catch handles the exception so the rest of the program continues. An uncaught exception ends the program with a stack trace.

Division by Zero

Source code
public class ZeroDivError{
    public static void main(String[] args){
        try{
            int c = 10 / 0;
            System.out.println("Result:"+c);
        }
        catch (ArithmeticException e){
            System.out.println("Error: Division by zero");
        }
        System.out.println("Code executed");
    }
}
Output
ERROR!
Error: Division by zero
Code executed

Common Exception Types

Source code
public class Exceptiontypes {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            int a = 5 / 0;
        } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
            System.out.println("Caught ArithmeticException: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        try {
            int[] arr = new int[3];
            int val = arr[5];
        } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
            System.out.println("Caught ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        try {
            String str = null;
            int length = str.length();
        } catch (NullPointerException e) {
            System.out.println("Caught NullPointerException: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Output
Caught ArithmeticException: / by zero
Caught ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 5 out of bounds for length 3
Caught NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "<local1>" is null

Uncaught Exception

Source code
public class UncaughtExceptionDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int num = 50 / 0; // Uncaught exception, terminates program and prints stack trace
        System.out.println("This line will not execute.");
    }
}
Output
ERROR!
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero
	at Main.main(Main.java:6)

Multiple catch Blocks

Several catch blocks handle different exception types; the first matching one runs, so specific types go before Exception.

Multiple catch Blocks

Source code
public class MultipleCatch{
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            String s = null;
            System.out.println(s.length()); // Triggers NullPointerException
            int x = 10 / 0;
        } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
            System.out.println("Arithmetic exception handled.");
        } catch (NullPointerException e) {
            System.out.println("Null pointer exception handled.");
        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.out.println("General exception handled.");
        }
    }
}
Output
Null pointer exception handled.

throw and throws

throw raises an exception explicitly; throws in a method signature declares that it may pass a checked exception to its caller.

Using throw

Source code
public class Throw{
    public static void checkAge(int age) {
        if (age < 18) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Age must be 18 or older.");
        } else {
            System.out.println("Access granted.");
        }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            checkAge(15);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Caught explicit exception: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Output
Caught explicit exception: Age must be 18 or older.

Using throws

Source code
import java.io.IOException;
public class Throws{
    static void validateFile() throws IOException {
        throw new IOException("Device error/File error.");
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            validateFile();
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.out.println("Caught propagated exception: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Output
Caught propagated exception: Device error/File error.

finally

The finally block always runs, whether or not an exception occurred, and is used for cleanup.

The finally Block

Source code
public class Finally{
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            int data = 25 / 5;
            System.out.println(data);
        } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
            System.out.println(e);
        } finally {
            System.out.println("Finally block is always executed.");
        }
    }
}
Output
5
Finally block is always executed.

User-Defined Exceptions

Extend Exception to create your own type for validation rules such as invalid age or marks.

User-Defined Exception

Source code
class InvalidAgeException extends Exception {
    public InvalidAgeException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}
public class UserDefinedException {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int age = 12;
        try {
            if (age < 18) {
                throw new InvalidAgeException("Not eligible to vote.");
            }
        } catch (InvalidAgeException e) {

}

Marks Validation with a Custom Exception

Source code
class InvalidMarksException extends Exception {
    public InvalidMarksException(String msg) {
        super(msg);
    }
}
public class MarksValidation {
    public static void validateMarks(int marks) throws InvalidMarksException {
        if (marks < 0 || marks > 100) {
            throw new InvalidMarksException("Marks must be between 0 and 100.");
        }
        System.out.println("Marks are valid: " + marks);
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            validateMarks(105);
        } catch (InvalidMarksException e) {
            System.out.println("Validation Error: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Output
Validation Error: Marks must be between 0 and 100.

Combined Exception Handling

Source code
class OutOfRangeEx extends Exception {
    OutOfRangeEx(String s) { super(s); }
}
public class AllExceptions {
    static void checkValue(int val) throws OutOfRangeEx {
        if (val > 50) {
            throw new OutOfRangeEx("Value exceeds limit 50.");
        }
        System.out.println("Valid value.");
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            int num = 10;
            int res = num / 2;
            checkValue(60); // Triggers custom exception
        } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
            System.out.println("Arithmetic caught.");
        } catch (OutOfRangeEx e) {
            System.out.println("Custom caught: " + e.getMessage());
        } finally {
            System.out.println("Finally block executed cleanly.");
        }
    }
}
Output
Custom caught: Value exceeds limit 50.
Finally block executed cleanly.

I/O: Byte Streams

Byte array streams, FileInputStream and FileOutputStream, copying files and images with a buffer.

The concept

Streams move data in and out of a program. Byte streams (InputStream/OutputStream, 8-bit) handle any binary data such as images and files.

Byte Array Streams

ByteArrayInputStream and ByteArrayOutputStream read and write bytes in memory.

Byte Array Streams

Source code
import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream;
import java.io.IOException;
public class ByteStream {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        byte[] data = {65, 66, 67, 68}; // ASCII for A, B, C, D
        ByteArrayInputStream input = new ByteArrayInputStream(data);
        ByteArrayOutputStream output = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
        int val;
        while ((val = input.read()) != -1) {
            output.write(val);
        }
        System.out.println("Output bytes as string: " + output.toString());
    }
}
Output
Output bytes as string: ABCD

Reading and Writing Files

FileInputStream reads bytes from a file and FileOutputStream writes them. Missing files or permissions raise IOException, shown in the logs below.

Reading a File Byte by Byte

Source code
import java.io.FileInputStream;
import java.io.IOException;
public class ReadFileByteByByte {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (FileInputStream fis = new FileInputStream("test.txt")) {
            int i;
            while ((i = fis.read()) != -1) {
                System.out.print((char) i);
            }
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.out.println("Error reading file: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Output
Error reading file: test.txt (No such file or directory)

Writing a File with FileOutputStream

Source code
import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.IOException;
public class WriteFileByte {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String text = "Learning Byte Streams in Java.";
        try (FileOutputStream fos = new FileOutputStream("output.txt")) {
            fos.write(text.getBytes());
            System.out.println("Data successfully written to output.txt");
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.out.println("Error writing file: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Output
Error writing file: output.txt (Permission denied)

Copying Files

Copy a file by reading and writing byte by byte, or faster with a byte[] buffer, which also works for images.

Copying a File Byte by Byte

Source code
import java.io.FileInputStream;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.IOException;
public class CopyFileBytes {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (FileInputStream fis = new FileInputStream("source.txt");
        FileOutputStream fos = new FileOutputStream("destination.txt")) {
            int temp;
            while ((temp = fis.read()) != -1) {
                fos.write(temp);
            }
            System.out.println("File copied successfully.");
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.out.println("I/O Error: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Output
ERROR!
I/O Error: source.txt (No such file or directory)

Copying an Image File with a Buffer

Source code
import java.io.FileInputStream;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.FileNotFoundException;
import java.io.IOException;
public class CopyImageBytes {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FileInputStream fis = null;
        FileOutputStream fos = null;
        try {
            fis = new FileInputStream("source_image.jpg");
            fos = new FileOutputStream("destination_image.jpg");
            byte[] buffer = new byte[1024];
            int length;
            while ((length = fis.read(buffer)) > 0) {
                fos.write(buffer, 0, length);
            }
            System.out.println("Image copied successfully using try-catch-finally.");
        } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
            System.out.println("File not found: " + e.getMessage());
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.out.println("I/O exception occurred: " + e.getMessage());
        } finally {
            try {
                if (fis != null) fis.close();
                if (fos != null) fos.close();
            } catch (IOException e) {
                System.out.println("Error closing streams: " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    }
}
Output
File not found: source_image.jpg (No such file or directory)

Character Streams and Threads

16-bit character streams, file reading and writing, and multithreading: Thread vs Runnable, isAlive() and join().

The concept

Character streams (Reader/Writer, 16-bit Unicode) are meant for text. A thread is an independent path of execution; Java supports multithreading by extending Thread or implementing Runnable.

Character Streams

InputStreamReader, FileReader and FileWriter read and write text as 16-bit characters. Try-with-resources closes the stream automatically.

Keyboard Input to Console

Source code
import java.io.InputStreamReader;
import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.io.Reader;
import java.io.Writer;
import java.io.IOException;
public class KeyboardToConsole {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Enter text (Press Ctrl+D or Ctrl+Z to stop):");
        try (Reader reader = new InputStreamReader(System.in);
        Writer writer = new PrintWriter(System.out)) {
            int character;
            while ((character = reader.read()) != -1) {
                writer.write(character);
                writer.flush();
            }
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.err.println("An I/O error occurred: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Counting Characters, Words and Lines

Source code
import java.io.FileReader;
import java.io.IOException;
public class FileCounterDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int charCount = 0;
        int wordCount = 0;
        int lineCount = 0;
        boolean inWord = false;
        try (FileReader reader = new FileReader("input.txt")) {
            int character;
            while ((character = reader.read()) != -1) {
                charCount++;
                char ch = (char) character;
                if (ch == '\n') {
                    lineCount++;
                }
                if (Character.isWhitespace(ch)) {
                    inWord = false;
                } else if (!inWord) {
                    wordCount++;
                    inWord = true;
                }
            }
            if (charCount > 0 && lineCount == 0) {
                lineCount = 1;
            }
            System.out.println("Characters: " + charCount);
            System.out.println("Words: " + wordCount);
            System.out.println("Lines: " + lineCount);
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.err.println("Error analyzing file: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Thread Control

Threads run concurrently, so their output interleaves. isAlive() checks whether a thread is running and join() makes one thread wait for another to finish.

Concurrent Execution of Threads

Source code
class InterleavedTask implements Runnable {
    @Override
    public void run() {
        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
            System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " processing item: " + i);
            try {
                Thread.sleep(100);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                System.out.println("Thread execution interrupted");
            }
        }
    }
}
public class ConcurrentExecution {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Thread t1 = new Thread(new InterleavedTask(), "Thread-A");
        Thread t2 = new Thread(new InterleavedTask(), "Thread-B");
        Thread t3 = new Thread(new InterleavedTask(), "Thread-C");
        t1.start();
        t2.start();
        t3.start();
    }
}
Output

Thread-B processing item: 2
Thread-A processing item: 3

Checking Threads with isAlive()

Source code
public class IsAliveDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread thread = new Thread(() -> {
            try { Thread.sleep(300); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) {}
        });
        System.out.println("Before start() - Is thread alive? " + thread.isAlive());
        thread.start();
        System.out.println("After start() - Is thread alive? " + thread.isAlive());
        thread.join();
        System.out.println("After completion - Is thread alive? " + thread.isAlive());
    }
}

After start() - Is thread alive? true
After completion - Is thread alive? False

Waiting for a Thread with join()

Source code
public class JoinMethod {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Thread dependentThread = new Thread(() -> {
            System.out.println("Dependent thread starting heavy computations...");
            try {
                Thread.sleep(1000);
                System.out.println("Dependent thread work finished.");
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                System.err.println(e.getMessage());
            }
        });
        dependentThread.start();
        System.out.println("Main thread waiting for dependent thread to conclude via join()...");
        try {
            dependentThread.join();
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            System.err.println(e.getMessage());
        }
        System.out.println("Main thread execution resumes and wraps up.");
    }
}
Output

Controlled Sequential Execution

Source code
public class ControlledExecution {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Runnable task = () -> {
            System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " has begun.");
            try { Thread.sleep(400); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) {}
            System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " has completed.");
        };
        Thread t1 = new Thread(task, "Stage-1");
        Thread t2 = new Thread(task, "Stage-2");
        Thread t3 = new Thread(task, "Stage-3");
        t1.start();
        System.out.println("Checking Stage-1 running status: " + t1.isAlive());
        t1.join();
        t2.start();
        t2.join();
        t3.start();
        t3.join();
        System.out.println("All controlled sequencing stages have completed successfully.");
    }
}

All controlled sequencing stages have completed successfully.
